facts.text: Fireworks are widely used around the world to celebrate big occasions such as New Year's Eve.
Gunpowder is a mixture of saltpeter (potassium nitrate), sulfur and charcoal that burns very fast with a flash.
Chinese alchemists probably found the gunpowder mixture by accident sometime between 600 and 900 CE while searching for a potion for eternal life.
Chinese makers filled bamboo with gunpowder to make some of the first manufactured fireworks, and later used paper tubes as well.
Early Chinese fireworks were used to frighten away evil spirits and to celebrate births and weddings.
Fireworks were already used for entertainment at China's imperial court by the 12th century.
Simple fireworks reached Europe around the 14th century.
For centuries the light of gunpowder fireworks was mostly orange, given off by tiny solid bits heated until they glowed.
Adding iron, copper or zinc filings could shift the color of early fireworks only slightly, toward yellow or white.
In medieval Europe, gunpowder displays were still limited to loud bangs and a few sparks.
In the 19th century potassium chlorate came into use in fireworks, bringing brilliant colors such as red and green and greater brightness.
Italian fireworks makers developed aerial shells in the 1830s and are credited with using metal powders to create specific colors.
Strontium compounds give red, calcium orange, sodium yellow, barium green and copper blue in fireworks.
The heat of a firework gives electrons in metal atoms extra energy and lifts them to a higher energy level; when they drop back they give off that energy as light.
The color of the light depends on the amount of energy released when an electron drops back.
Each element has its own set of energy jumps, so the colors it gives off act like a fingerprint that can identify the element, as in flame tests.
Blue is generally considered the most difficult firework color to produce.
